Chapter one. What you really own.

The most popular index for European ETF investors is the M S C I World. It holds over thirteen hundred companies, in twenty-three developed countries.

Together with its bigger cousins, the All-World and A C W I funds, it sits behind millions of savings plans, from Germany to Spain, from France to the Netherlands.

European ETFs now hold a record three point nine seven trillion dollars. And this year alone, investors added three hundred and eighty one billion more.

Most of that money flows into the same handful of global index funds. So what's actually inside them matters to a lot of people.

That sounds diversified. But the index is weighted by size. The bigger a company, the more of your money goes into it.

So let's follow one hundred euros into a world ETF today. Every square is one euro.

More than seventy of them go to American companies.

And about twenty-seven euros go to just ten companies.

Put differently: if those ten companies fell by half tomorrow, your whole world ETF would lose about thirteen percent, even if every other company on Earth stood perfectly still.

Who are they? Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Broadcom, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta. The names behind almost every AI headline.

Nvidia alone is valued at around five point three trillion dollars. That's more than every listed company in Germany put together.

And this concentration is new. Not long ago, the five biggest companies were around six percent of the world index. By the end of 2024, they were close to twenty percent.

The technology sector went from about a tenth of the index to more than a quarter in ten years.

To be clear, none of this is a conspiracy. It's simply how market cap indices work. When a company grows, you automatically own more of it.

And it's exactly why world ETFs did so well over the last decade. You rode the winners all the way up.

Think about what that means. You never had to pick Nvidia. The index picked it for you, and kept adding more as the price went up.

There's no rule in a market cap index that says: this is getting too expensive, let's take some money off the table. Price goes up, weight goes up. That's it.

But it works in both directions. When a giant falls, it falls with your money inside it.

The E C B economists put it bluntly. Looking at past technology revolutions, a correction is likely, and euro area households would feel it mostly through their funds.

Quick question before we go back in time.

In the year 2000, at the peak of the dot-com bubble, what share of the S and P five hundred did its ten largest companies make up?

Fifteen, twenty-six, or forty percent? Think about it. It was about twenty-six percent.

Today? It's close to forty. Higher than at the peak of the dot-com bubble.
